purpose: Phase 9 Step 11 - formal worst-case boundedness derivation for the research-loop product path (MedAgent(research_loop=True)), built from real constants read directly from source, not estimated.

MAX_TOOL_CALLS_TOTAL.note: counts research_execution_node INVOCATIONS (1 per follow-up iteration), not raw tool calls executed - looser/redundant vs MAX_RESEARCH_ITERATIONS=3, which binds first in practice (3 iterations reached long before 8 invocations could occur, since at most 1 invocation happens per iteration).

DECLARED_TOOLS_COUNT.note: SOFT practical per-round tool-call ceiling, not a hard schema/code cap - nothing in tool_orchestration_node's processing of raw_tool_calls limits how many distinct tool_calls a single Cerebras response may return; 6 is the number of distinct declared functions, and duplicate calls to the same function with different arguments are not structurally prevented.

LLM_CALL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS.applies_to: NVIDIA ChatNVIDIA calls (synthesis_node, report_generation_node, verification_node[legacy only])

CEREBRAS_FREE_TRIAL_RATE_LIMIT_RPM.source: shared bucket key 'cerebras_free_trial' used by generator.py, judge.py, nlu/extractor.py

call_graph_model.R_total_orchestration_rounds: 1 (initial) + MAX_RESEARCH_ITERATIONS = 1 + 3 = 4 (query_analysis->tool_orchestration is the initial round; research_execution_node re-invokes tool_orchestration_node once per follow-up iteration, up to 3 times)
call_graph_model.G_generation_gap_cycles: Same as R = 4: grounded_generation_node/gap_analysis_node run once after the initial evidence_normalization, then once per follow-up iteration after evidence_merge_node (build_research_loop_graph's edges: research_execution->evidence_merge->grounded_generation, bypassing synthesis_node on follow-up rounds).
call_graph_model.synthesis_node_calls: Exactly 1 per request - only reachable via the initial tool_orchestration->synthesis edge; the follow-up loop never revisits synthesis_node.
call_graph_model.report_generation_node_calls: Exactly 1 per request - reached once, after finalize_research_answer_node, regardless of stop reason.
call_graph_model.query_analysis_node_calls: Exactly 1 per request - the graph's single entry point, never revisited.

1_max_llm_calls_per_request.bounded_component: 1 (NLU query_analysis) + 4 (Cerebras tool-selection, 1 per orchestration round x R=4) + 1 (synthesis, NVIDIA) + 4 (grounded_generation, Cerebras, 1 per G=4 cycles) + 1 (report_generation, NVIDIA) = 11 logical LLM call SITES.
1_max_llm_calls_per_request.unbounded_component: + sum_{g=1..4} C_g, where C_g = number of FACTUAL claims with >=1 evidence_ids in cycle g's GroundedAnswer - each triggers exactly one judge_claim_semantic() call in analyze_gaps(). No code-level maximum exists on C_g (see claim_count_boundedness below).
1_max_llm_calls_per_request.is_finite: NO - unbounded as a function of model output length per generation call.

2_max_biomedical_source_calls_per_reques.formula: source_calls_max = R * DECLARED_TOOLS_COUNT = 4 * 6 = 24 (SOFT bound - see DECLARED_TOOLS_COUNT note; not a hard schema-enforced ceiling)
2_max_biomedical_source_calls_per_reques.is_finite: Practically yes (soft, model-behavior-dependent bound); not formally hard-capped in code.

3_max_retry_amplified_source_calls.formula: source_calls_max * (TOOL_MAX_RETRIES + 1) = 24 * 4 = 96 total HTTP attempts across all biomedical source calls, worst case.
3_max_retry_amplified_source_calls.is_finite: Yes, for a fixed source_calls_max (itself a soft bound per #2).

4_max_research_rounds.formula: R = 1 + MAX_RESEARCH_ITERATIONS = 1 + 3 = 4 total orchestration rounds (1 initial + <=3 follow-up iterations), hard-enforced by decide_stop_reason's BUDGET_EXHAUSTED check at iteration >= MAX_RESEARCH_ITERATIONS.

5_max_gap_analysis_judge_calls.formula: judge_calls_max = sum_{g=1}^{4} C_g (each factual claim in each of the 4 generation cycles triggers exactly one judge_claim_semantic call, per research/gap_analysis.py's 'for claim in grounded_answer.claims:' loop with no cap).
5_max_gap_analysis_judge_calls.is_finite: NO - see claim_count_boundedness section. This is PHASE9-DEFECT-001.

6_max_total_external_calls.unbounded_component: + sum_{g=1}^{4} C_g x <=2 attempts (Cerebras judge bounded retry) = up to 2 * sum(C_g)
6_max_total_external_calls.is_finite: NO - dominated by the same unbounded claim-count term.

bounded_component_breakdown_seconds.nvidia_synthesis: <=3 attempts x 90s + backoff(attempt0+attempt1, <=1s+2s worst case with jitter) ~= 270 + 3 = 273
bounded_component_breakdown_seconds.biomedical_source_http: 24 calls x [<=4 attempts x 30s + backoff(3 gaps, each min(2^k,60)*jitter, k=0..2 -> <=1+2+4=7s worst case per call)] ~= 24 x (120 + 7) = 3048

7_max_timeout_driven_wall_clock_time.bounded_total_seconds: ~120 + 240 + 273 + 3048 + 480 + 273 + 10.3 + 168 ~= 4612 seconds (~77 minutes) worst-case if EVERY individual call independently maxed out every attempt/timeout/backoff simultaneously - a pathological, not typical, case; real observed Phase-9 baseline cases ranged 58s-603s (see artifacts/v2/phase9_baseline_results.json).
7_max_timeout_driven_wall_clock_time.unbounded_component: + sum_{g=1}^{4} C_g x (<=2 attempts x 60s judge timeout + Cerebras-bucket rate-limit spacing ~12s/attempt) ~= sum(C_g) x ~144s per claim, worst case
7_max_timeout_driven_wall_clock_time.is_finite: NO, precisely because the call-COUNT term (sum of C_g) is unbounded, even though every INDIVIDUAL call/attempt/backoff/rate-limit-wait in the system is itself individually finite and bounded. There is no outer 'max request duration' deadline anywhere in the code that would independently cap total wall-clock regardless of call count - none was invented here; its absence is confirmed by grep (no timeout/deadline wrapping graph.invoke() in agent/graph.py::MedAgent.run(), only the LangGraph recursion_limit, which bounds NODE VISITS, not wall-clock time).

claim_count_boundedness.question: Does GroundedAnswer.claims have a schema maximum, generation maximum, parser maximum, validation maximum, or runtime maximum anywhere in the code?
claim_count_boundedness.answer: NO - confirmed absent at every one of the 4 layers checked.

evidence.finding: GroundedAnswer.claims: List[GroundedClaim] - a plain List[...] type annotation with NO Field(max_length=...) or any other length constraint. Confirmed by direct reading; grep for 'max_length' or 'max_items' anywhere in generation/models.py returns zero matches.

evidence.layer: generation JSON schema (the strict-mode contract sent to Cerebras)
evidence.finding: _CLAIMS_JSON_SCHEMA's 'claims' property is {'type': 'array', 'items': {...}} with NO 'maxItems' key. Confirmed by direct reading; grep for 'maxItems' anywhere in generation/generator.py returns zero matches.
claims_raw is checked only for being a list (isinstance(claims_raw, list)) and each entry is passed through GroundedClaim(**c) construction - no length check before or after parsing.

validate_claims() checks: (1) every evidence_id reference is known, (2) every FACTUAL claim has >=1 evidence_ids, (3) claim_id uniqueness, (4) no bare source-native ID citation. It performs NO check on len(claims) - confirmed by direct reading of the full function body.

'for claim in grounded_answer.claims:' iterates the ENTIRE claims list with no slicing, no early-exit cap, no sampling - every factual claim with evidence_ids triggers one judge_claim_semantic() call.

claim_count_boundedness.soft_mitigating_factor_not_a_cap: generation/generator.py's _invoke_cerebras_claims uses max_completion_tokens=4096 (pipeline default) for the Cerebras claim-generation call, which places an INDIRECT, TOKEN-BUDGET-DERIVED ceiling on total output size - but this is not a deterministic claim-COUNT cap: a model could produce many short claims (e.g. one-sentence claims each citing one evidence_id) within a 4096-token budget, and nothing in the code validates or rejects an unusually large claims array as a distinct failure mode. This does not change the conclusion that no genuine count-based cap exists.
claim_count_boundedness.conclusion: CORRECTED per the pre-optimization consistency audit: the system is NOT mathematically unbounded when the actually-executed max_completion_tokens=4096 provider ceiling is accounted for. It IS, however, missing any INTENTIONAL, semantically-meaningful application-level claim-evaluation budget - the only ceiling that exists is an accidental byproduct of a token-length setting chosen for unrelated reasons, and its real numeric value (order ~100-150 claims/cycle, ~400-600 across G=4 cycles) is large enough to provide no meaningful reliability guarantee for planning/timeout-budget purposes. This is reframed as an APPLICATION-LEVEL BOUNDEDNESS DEFECT / MISSING CLAIM-EVALUATION BUDGET, not a literal mathematical-infinity claim.
claim_count_boundedness.defect_title: Missing intentional application-level claim-evaluation budget for gap-analysis judge calls (the only existing ceiling is an incidental, very large, provider-token-budget side effect - not a deliberate reliability safeguard)
claim_count_boundedness.defect_classification: APPLICATION-LEVEL BOUNDEDNESS DEFECT (reframed from the original 'unbounded 'call-count claim per the pre-optimization consistency audit) - a real Phase-9 finding, not a literal-infinity overclaim; not a correctness/fabrication defect (no fabricated/invalid Evidence ID or silent failure was found anywhere in this pass's fault matrix).

candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.remedy: Hard max factual claims per answer (e.g. reject/truncate a generation exceeding N claims)
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.safety: Safe to implement in isolation - a simple post-generation length check.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.semantic_effect: Could silently discard legitimate claims for an answer that genuinely needs many (e.g. a broad multi-drug-class query with many independently-cited facts) unless truncation is disclosed to the user.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.compatibility_with_frozen_phase6_7_behav: Would require touching generation/validation.py or generation/pipeline.py, both frozen Phase-6 artifacts - any change needs its own gate re-review, not a Phase-9-internal decision.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.grounding_quality_impact: None if claims are truncated by lowest-priority/least-confident (not evaluated by this pass); could reduce completeness if truncation is arbitrary (e.g. simple list slicing).
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.latency_impact: Reduces worst-case gap-analysis latency directly and predictably (bounded judge-call count).
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.silent_drop_risk: HIGH if not paired with explicit disclosure (a dropped/truncated claim must never look like a claim that was never produced) - would need its own qualifier/caveat mechanism, echoing PHASE8-DEFECT-001's fix pattern (finalize_research_answer_node's qualifier propagation).
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.user_visible_behavior_change: Yes - answers that would have had more than N claims would visibly shrink.

candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.remedy: Total gap-analysis evaluation BUDGET (cap total judge calls across the whole request, not per-answer)
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.safety: Safe - a simple running counter compared against a constant, similar in spirit to MAX_TOOL_CALLS_TOTAL's existing pattern.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.semantic_effect: Once the budget is exhausted, some claims would go un-judged - gap_analysis would need an explicit 'not evaluated' state distinct from 'evaluated and supported', so it is never confused with a false SUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE stop.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.compatibility_with_frozen_phase6_7_behav: Does not touch generation/ at all - purely a research/gap_analysis.py + research/loop_control.py change, which are Phase-8-owned (already understood to be extensible for Phase-9-discovered defects per the governing directive's carve-out).
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.grounding_quality_impact: Un-judged claims would neither be confirmed supported nor flagged weak - a real quality-signal gap, needs disclosure.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.latency_impact: Directly bounds worst-case gap-analysis wall-clock time - the most surgical fix for formula #7's unbounded term.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.silent_drop_risk: MEDIUM - the claims themselves are not dropped (still rendered in the answer), only their gap-analysis judgment is skipped; risk is a claim silently NOT being flagged weak/contradicted because its judge call never ran, which could look like a false 'this claim was checked and is fine'.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.user_visible_behavior_change: Only if disclosed - otherwise invisible (the answer text is unchanged, only internal gap detection is capped).

candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.remedy: Batch claim judging (one Cerebras call judges MULTIPLE claims at once, not one call per claim)
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.safety: Safe in principle - would need a new JSON schema (array of claim+judgment pairs) and careful evidence-block sizing (a batched prompt with many claims' cited Evidence could itself exceed practical context/token limits, trading claim-count unboundedness for prompt-size unboundedness unless ALSO capped).
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.semantic_effect: None if the judge's per-claim semantics are preserved faithfully in the batched schema - would need its own validation pass, out of Phase-9 scope to design here.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.compatibility_with_frozen_phase6_7_behav: grounding_eval/judge.py is a Phase-7-frozen artifact (judge_claim_semantic is explicitly 'the same evaluator Phase 7 froze and validated' per research/gap_analysis.py's own docstring) - changing its call shape would require its own re-validation pass, not a Phase-9-internal decision.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.grounding_quality_impact: Unknown without re-validation - batched judging could change the judge's own accuracy (more context per call, but less isolated attention per claim) and would need the same rigor as Phase 7's original Candidate B vs Candidate E comparison before being trusted.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.latency_impact: Would reduce the NUMBER of calls (one call for many claims) but each call would take longer and use more tokens - net latency effect is unmeasured, not assumed.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.silent_drop_risk: LOW if batch responses are validated to cover every submitted claim_id exactly once (similar to today's per-claim try/except-skip-on-failure pattern).
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.user_visible_behavior_change: None expected if judgments are semantically equivalent - but unverified without a dedicated measurement pass.

candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.remedy: Bounded concurrency (issue judge calls for multiple claims in parallel, up to a fixed worker count)
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.safety: Safe from a correctness standpoint if each judge call remains independent (it is - judge_claim_semantic takes only claim text + cited Evidence, no shared mutable state beyond the already-audited rate limiter/HTTP session).
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.semantic_effect: None - does not change WHAT is computed, only WHEN/how many calls run concurrently.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.compatibility_with_frozen_phase6_7_behav: Compatible - judge_claim_semantic itself is unchanged; only its caller (research/gap_analysis.py::analyze_gaps) would change from sequential to a bounded thread/task pool.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.grounding_quality_impact: None (same judge, same inputs, same outputs, only concurrency of invocation changes).
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.latency_impact: Directly reduces WALL-CLOCK time proportionally to worker count for a FIXED claim count, but does NOT change the total CALL COUNT or rate-limiter contention (Cerebras 5 RPM bucket would still serialize actual dispatch regardless of how many threads are waiting) - so this reduces latency only up to the rate limiter's own ceiling, and does nothing for formula #5's unbounded call-COUNT problem.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.silent_drop_risk: LOW if implemented correctly (a bounded thread pool with proper result collection).
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.explicitly_out_of_scope_this_pass: The governing directive explicitly forbids parallelizing gap_analysis in THIS pass - listed here only as a candidate for future evaluation, not evaluated further or implemented.

candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.remedy: Bounded truncation with explicit safe behavior (cap claims array length at generation time, always with a disclosed truncation marker/qualifier)
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.safety: Safe if the truncation marker is itself validated as present whenever truncation occurs (a testable invariant).
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.semantic_effect: Directly analogous to Option A but with the disclosure requirement built in from the start rather than as an afterthought - the answer would explicitly state '(N additional claims omitted)' or similar.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.compatibility_with_frozen_phase6_7_behav: Same concern as Option A - touches generation/pipeline.py or generation/validation.py, both frozen, needing its own gate review.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.grounding_quality_impact: Completeness would visibly decrease for answers that would have exceeded the cap - an honest tradeoff, not a silent one, IF implemented with the disclosure requirement.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.latency_impact: Same direct benefit as Option A.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.silent_drop_risk: LOW by construction (this option's entire premise IS the disclosure requirement) - the safest of the generation-side options if a cap must be added there.

candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.remedy: Whole-answer gap analysis instead of one-call-per-claim (a single judge call evaluates the ENTIRE GroundedAnswer against its full cited-Evidence set, not each claim independently)
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.safety: Safe from a call-count-boundedness standpoint (exactly 1 call per generation cycle, i.e. exactly G=4 total judge calls, hard-bounded) - but changes the GRANULARITY of what is judged.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.semantic_effect: SIGNIFICANT - loses per-claim gap_id/related_claim_id attribution, which research/action_planning.py's plan_actions() and finalize_research_answer_node's per-claim qualifier mechanism (PHASE8-DEFECT-001's fix) both depend on. Would require redesigning the EvidenceGap.related_claim_id linkage entirely, not a drop-in swap.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.compatibility_with_frozen_phase6_7_behav: Would replace, not extend, grounding_eval/judge.py's frozen per-claim judge_claim_semantic contract - the most invasive of the 6 options relative to Phase-7's frozen validation.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.grounding_quality_impact: Unknown and likely negative for precision - a whole-answer judgment could not surface WHICH specific claim is weak/contradicted, undermining the existing targeted-follow-up mechanism (research/action_planning.py's whole design is gap-to-claim-to-followup-query, all keyed by claim_id).
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.latency_impact: Best-case reduction (hard-bounded at G=4 total judge calls, independent of claim count) - the strongest latency fix of all 6 options.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.silent_drop_risk: MEDIUM-HIGH - a whole-answer judgment that says 'partially supported' with no claim-level attribution risks looking like a real, specific finding while actually being a coarser, less actionable one; would need very careful qualifier language to avoid implying more precision than it has.
candidate_remedies_analyzed_not_implemen.user_visible_behavior_change: Indirect - the final answer's caveat/qualifier granularity would likely become coarser (whole-answer caveats instead of per-claim ones).

claim_count_boundedness.pre_optimization_audit_correction: The original conclusion ('UNBOUNDED') did not check whether an executed provider-side output-token limit indirectly bounds claim count even though no application-level cap exists. Rechecked: generation/generator.py's _invoke_cerebras_claims sends max_completion_tokens=4096 (its own hard-coded default, confirmed by reading its single call site at generate_grounded_answer -> line 243 - with NO override anywhere in the executed path) inside the actual Cerebras chat-completions request body, using strict JSON-schema mode (response_format.json_schema.strict=True). Standard OpenAI-compatible completions-API behavior (which Cerebras implements) hard-truncates generation at that token count - a real, provider-enforced, executed ceiling, not an invented one.

answers.D_strongest_defensible_statement: OUTCOME #2 of the 3 offered: finite ONLY because of the external/provider max_completion_tokens=4096 output-token ceiling on the Cerebras claim-generation call - NOT because of any deliberate application-level claims budget. Outcome #1 ('truly unbounded') is an overclaim and is WITHDRAWN. Outcome #3 ('a finite application-level bound already exists and was missed') is also false - no code enforces a claim COUNT; only an incidental token-length setting chosen for unrelated cost/latency reasons happens to cap it.
answers.order_of_magnitude_estimate_of_the_finit: Using each GroundedClaim's required JSON fields (text, evidence_ids, claim_type enum, qualifier) at their most minimal encoding (short text, one short evidence_id, e.g. '{"text":"X.","evidence_ids":["E1"],"claim_type":"factual","qualifier":null}' ~25-35 tokens including JSON punctuation/array overhead), 4096 tokens for the WHOLE response (also containing the wrapping object and conflict_detected field) yields an order-of-magnitude ceiling on the order of ~100-150 claims per generation cycle. This is DISCLOSED AS AN ORDER-OF-MAGNITUDE ESTIMATE, not an exact enforced count - actual capacity depends on real evidence_id string length and claim text content, and is NOT independently re-measured empirically in this pass (no live call was made to verify it, per this pass's own no-live-call constraint). A bounded 2-attempt retry on generation failure does not increase this per-cycle ceiling (a retry replaces, never accumulates with, a prior attempt's claims).

time_bound_analysis.finding: Every INDIVIDUAL external call, retry attempt, backoff sleep, and rate-limit wait in the system IS finitely bounded (confirmed by direct reading of every timeout/retry-count/backoff-max/rate-limit constant across config/llm_config.py, orchestration/candidate_b_native_tools.py, grounding_eval/judge.py, generation/generator.py, nlu/extractor.py, utils/retry_handler.py, utils/rate_limiter.py). Research-loop ITERATIONS are also hard-bounded (MAX_RESEARCH_ITERATIONS=3, enforced by research/loop_control.py::decide_stop_reason, proven non-infinite by existing tests). HOWEVER, the total NUMBER of gap-analysis judge calls issued within each of those bounded iterations is NOT bounded, because it is driven by GroundedAnswer.claims' length, which has no cap anywhere in the code (see claim_count_boundedness above). Therefore: the system does NOT currently have a finite, code-enforced wall-clock upper bound on a single request - not because any wait/call path is itself unbounded, but because the TOTAL NUMBER of otherwise-individually-bounded calls is unbounded. No 'max request duration' deadline of any kind exists in the code (confirmed by grep across agent/graph.py, agent/nodes.py, research/*.py for any wrapping timeout/deadline around graph.invoke() or the research loop as a whole) - none is invented or assumed here.
individually_bounded_paths_confirmed: NVIDIA ChatNVIDIA calls: 90s x <=3 attempts, hard daemon-thread-enforced timeout
Cerebras tool-selection calls: 60s x 1 attempt (never retried)
Cerebras generator/judge/NLU calls: 60s x <=2 attempts each
Tool HTTP calls: 30s x <=4 attempts + backoff (base=2s, max=60s per gap)
Rate-limiter waits: bounded by TokenBucket's own bounded refill math for ANY fixed number of calls (unbounded only insofar as the NUMBER of calls needing tokens is unbounded)
time_bound_analysis.unbounded_path: The count of judge_claim_semantic() invocations per gap_analysis_node call (research/gap_analysis.py line 84's uncapped 'for claim in grounded_answer.claims' loop), which is itself driven by the uncapped GroundedAnswer.claims length (PHASE9-DEFECT-001).
time_bound_analysis.precise_statement: All individual calls are bounded; the TOTAL NUMBER of calls is not, due exclusively to the claim-count issue. This is a call-count boundedness gap, not a per-call timeout gap - no per-call path was found to hang indefinitely or retry without limit.

tool_vs_source_call_reconciliation.question: What does DECLARED_TOOLS_COUNT=6 represent vs MAX_TOOL_CALLS_TOTAL=8? Are they the same layer? Does one supersede the other?
tool_vs_source_call_reconciliation.DECLARED_TOOLS_COUNT_6: orchestration/candidate_b_native_tools.py's DECLARED_TOOLS tuple - the number of DISTINCT tool FUNCTION SCHEMAS offered to Cerebras's native tool-calling API in a single tool-selection request. It is NOT an enforced ceiling on how many tool_call entries a single Cerebras response may return - confirmed by reading agent/nodes.py's tool_orchestration_node: 'for i, raw_call in enumerate(raw_tool_calls):' has no length check. Nothing prevents the model from returning duplicate calls to the same function, or an unusually long tool_calls array, in one response.
tool_vs_source_call_reconciliation.MAX_TOOL_CALLS_TOTAL_8: research/loop_control.py's hard application-level counter, but it counts research_execution_node INVOCATIONS (one per follow-up ROUND: agent/nodes.py:1625 increments state['research_tool_calls_used'] exactly once per research_execution_node call, regardless of how many individual tool calls that round's tool_orchestration_node execution actually made) - NOT individual biomedical tool/source calls. It operates at the ROUND layer, not the per-round-tool-call layer.
tool_vs_source_call_reconciliation.one_supersedes_the_other: Yes: MAX_RESEARCH_ITERATIONS=3 (giving R=4 total rounds: 1 initial + <=3 follow-ups) is the binding constraint on round count, since at most 1 research_execution_node invocation happens per iteration. research_tool_calls_used can therefore reach at most 3 (one per follow-up), never approaching MAX_TOOL_CALLS_TOTAL=8 - MAX_TOOL_CALLS_TOTAL=8 is LOOSER than R and never binds under the current loop structure (effectively dead/redundant, as already flagged in the original constants_used note).
tool_vs_source_call_reconciliation.conflation_found: Yes - the original report's '24' and '96' formulas treated DECLARED_TOOLS_COUNT=6 as if it were a HARD per-round cap on individual tool_calls (giving a clean-looking R x 6 = 24), when it is only the count of distinct declared FUNCTION NAMES, not an enforced limit on how many tool_call entries (valid or not) a round's Cerebras response may contain. Additionally, 'tool calls' (raw model output entries) and 'source calls' (actual biomedical HTTP requests) were conflated: a tool_call that fails registry validation (unregistered_tool/arguments_json_invalid/schema_invalid - see fault-matrix scenarios A9-A11) NEVER reaches an HTTP call at all, so logical tool_calls attempted is properly an UPPER bound on actual source HTTP calls issued, not an equality.
tool_vs_source_call_reconciliation.corrected_per_round_tool_call_ceiling: Like the claims-per-cycle case, the ACTUAL executed ceiling on tool_call entries per round is soft and provider-token-budget-derived: orchestration/candidate_b_native_tools.py's call_cerebras_native_tools uses max_completion_tokens=1024 (default, confirmed no override at its single call site, agent/nodes.py:641). Using the same order-of-magnitude reasoning as the claims analysis (each tool_call entry needs a function name + JSON arguments, on the order of tens of tokens), the per-round ceiling is an order-of-magnitude estimate around ~20-30 valid tool_calls, NOT a clean hard-coded '6'.
tool_vs_source_call_reconciliation.true_source_call_maximum: NOT a single clean hard number. R=4 (hard application constant, from MAX_RESEARCH_ITERATIONS) x per-round-valid-tool-calls (soft, provider-token-budget-bounded, order-of-magnitude ~20-30) = a SOFT, INPUT/OUTPUT-DEPENDENT order-of-magnitude estimate of roughly 80-120 logical biomedical calls per request - NOT the previously-stated hard-sounding '24'. MAX_TOOL_CALLS_TOTAL=8 does not participate in this formula at all (it counts rounds, already captured by R=4, and never binds tighter than R does).

model_a_closed_workload.description: A finite, known set of N callers arrive once and all wait on the same bucket.
model_a_closed_workload.can_a_specific_caller_be_starved: No in practice for this codebase's actual usage pattern (a handful of concurrent tasks, single process) - with a fixed N and no NEW callers ever joining, every caller eventually gets a token because the bucket keeps refilling at its configured rate and the total token supply over any sufficiently long window exceeds N.
model_a_closed_workload.is_wait_finitely_bounded: Yes, for a closed/fixed N: worst case is (N-1) x (1/rate) seconds for the last-scheduled caller, since the unordered spin-wait can only ever make a caller wait behind at most the other N-1 callers' worth of token consumption before the bucket's own deterministic refill math guarantees it a token.
model_a_closed_workload.assumption_required: N is fixed and finite, and no NEW caller ever joins after the initial N.

model_b_arbitrary_sustained_arrivals.description: New callers can arrive continuously and indefinitely while earlier callers are still waiting.
model_b_arbitrary_sustained_arrivals.can_a_specific_caller_be_starved: Yes, in principle - wait_for_token()'s unordered spin-wait (confirmed via source reading: no FIFO queue, no ordering guarantee) means a newly-arriving thread can win a freshly-refilled token before an earlier-arrived, still-waiting thread does, with no fairness mechanism preventing this from recurring indefinitely under sustained new arrivals.
model_b_arbitrary_sustained_arrivals.is_wait_finitely_bounded: NOT universally, under this model. No per-caller maximum wait time is derivable without an additional assumption bounding the arrival rate/pattern of new callers relative to the bucket's refill rate.
model_b_arbitrary_sustained_arrivals.assumption_required: A universal finite bound requires ASSUMING either (a) a maximum caller arrival rate strictly less than the bucket's refill rate over any window (so the queue doesn't grow unboundedly), or (b) a fixed, closed set of callers (Model A) - neither of which is enforced or guaranteed anywhere in the code for Model B.

rate_limiter_starvation_analysis.corrected_conclusion: The original report's blanket 'rate-limit wait is finite' claim (used inside formula #7's wall-clock derivation) is accurate ONLY under Model A (this codebase's actual current usage pattern: a fixed, small, known number of concurrent MedAgent() tasks per process, confirmed via evaluation/evaluator.py's fresh-instance-per-task pattern - there is no code path today that admits an arbitrary, unbounded stream of NEW concurrent callers into the same rate limiter). It is NOT a universal claim independent of workload model, and should not be read as one.
rate_limiter_starvation_analysis.classification: Under Model A (this codebase's actual current usage): a documented scheduling property, not a defect - fairness/ordering was never claimed or required for this project's actual (single-process, small-N) concurrency profile. Under Model B (a hypothetical future arbitrary-arrival-rate scenario, e.g. a multi-tenant service): this WOULD be a reliability/boundedness gap requiring remediation (a fairness/queueing mechanism) before that scenario could rely on a finite per-request wait guarantee - but Model B does not describe this codebase's current, tested usage, so it is NOT classified as a Phase-9 defect requiring remediation now. Flagged as a documented assumption/limitation instead.

claim_budget_design.scope: REQUEST-GLOBAL (across all G<=4 generation cycles), not per-cycle
scope_rationale: Directly bounds the actual reliability concern (total judge-call count / wall-clock cost for the WHOLE request) with one clean number.
Matches the existing request-global-budget naming convention already established by MAX_TOOL_CALLS_TOTAL in the same module.
A per-cycle-only budget would still need multiplying by the hard cycle count to produce a request-level guarantee, so request-global is the more direct choice, not a more complex one.
claim_budget_design.derivation: observed single-round max claims in the primary Phase-8 dev/validation corpus (8, n=45 round-level values) x hard MAX_RESEARCH_ITERATIONS-derived cycle count (G=4) = 32 - exactly what a request would need to sustain the corpus's own worst observed single-round rate across every one of its hard-bounded cycles. Already 2x the highest actually-observed CUMULATIVE multi-round total in that same corpus (16, case VAL-F-tool-failure-safe-termination).

derivation.MAX_TOOL_CALLS_PER_ROUND: 2x DECLARED_TOOLS_COUNT=6 - headroom for the model to legitimately call the same tool twice with different arguments in one round; coincidentally already covers the single highest real aggregate-per-request n_tool_calls value observed (12, artifacts/v2/phase9_baseline_results.json's F5-research-loop-one-followup case) even under the pessimistic assumption it all concentrated in one round. design_decision_invalid_calls_consume_bu.decision: Invalid (registry-rejected) raw_tool_calls[] entries DO consume a budget slot, counted the moment they appear in the array, before parse_and_validate_tool_call ever runs on them.
design_decision_invalid_calls_consume_bu.rationale: The alternative (only registry-valid calls consume budget) would let a response padded with many registry-invalid junk entries bypass the budget's real purpose: bounding total processing effort spent on a round's raw model output, not just how many calls reach the HTTP boundary. This is the more conservative, smallest-blast-radius choice.

overflow_semantics: Overflow entries NEVER parsed, NEVER validated, NEVER executed, NEVER given a fabricated ToolResult.
Truncation preserves Cerebras's own returned order exactly - no reordering/prioritization.
